Contact: isaac.qs@csuci.edu

Exposure to several data acquisition, storage, and management techniques using appropriate computer software. Topics include query languages, relational databases, API access, data scraping, unstructured data sources, data security, and large data systems.




Use programming tools to construct a data set from separate databases.
Write programs to scrape webpages to construct a data set for analysis.
Differentiate between structured, unstructured, and semistructured data sources.
Explain how to access data from a website’s application program interface.
Describe the security and ethical implications of utilizing sensitive data sources.




Throughout this course, students will use the following software and programming environments:



Positron (Recommended) provides free and open source tools for your data analysis in R and/or Python. You may download positron here.
VS Code provides tools for software development as well as data analysis. You may download VS Code here.
VS Codium is the freely-licensed version of VS Code. You may download VS Codium here.





SQLite — primary relational database system (file-based)
MongoDB — primary document-based NoSQL database

Course Assignments

Course Project
Working in a group of up to 2 students, you will explore a Database Management System (DBMS) that was not used in the course. The goal is to apply the database concepts and skills developed throughout the semester to a new database environment and to evaluate how the selected system compares with the tools used in class.


Weekly Reports
Weekly reports are progress reports submitted to the instructor to keep track of your progress in completeing the course project. Each week, you will submit what you accomplished in the previous week, any challenges you faced, how you overcame those challenges, and your goal for next week (SMART goal). These will be weekly assignments. Three progress reports will be dropped at the end of the semester. Progress Reports are due every Saturday at 11:59 PM. There will be no make ups for progress reports.


Video Assignments
Videos are used to teach data management concepts related to the course. Students are expected to watch at least one video a week. The videos are implemented using PlayPosit. The 3 lowest video assignments will be dropped. Video assignments will be due every Sunday at 11:59 PM.


In-Class Assignments
In-class assignments are designed for you to practice different fundamentals related to data management. You are expected to complete the assignments every week and submit them every Sunday at 11:59 PM. The three lowest assignments will be dropped.



Generative Artificial Intelligence Policy
The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in an ethical manner is permitted for this course.

Permitted Uses
You may use AI for:

Obtain clarification
Brainstorming ideas, examples, outlines, and strategies
Generating questions for practice or exploration
Identifying keywords or phrasing to match professional goals



Prohibited Uses
You may not:

Submit AI-generated work
Use AI to complete assignments, quizzes, exams, or other assessments meant to reflect your own work

Any AI-generated work will receive a 0 in the class. Severe cases will be reported to Academic Misconduct.
You may not upload any course material to any AI platforms such as, but not limited to, ChatGPT, Claude, Github Copilot, Meta AI, or Google Gemini. Exceptions are allowed for DASS-approved services.

Use of Generative AI Policy
The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) to complete any part or all of an assignment/exam is strictly prohibited in this class. This includes, but not limited to, ChatGPT, Claude, Meta AI, and Google Gemini.

You may use AI to enhance you understanding of the material.


You may not use AI to complete assignments.


You may not upload any course material to any AI platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, Meta AI, and Google Gemini. Exceptions are allowed for DASS-approved services.

title: Data 300
text:
Use of AI
There are consequences when you use of AI:

Educational Mislearning
Trusting AI
Stolen Work
Privacy Concerns
Environmental Impacts
Working Exploitation

title: Data 300
text:
Educational Mislearning
The purpose of this class, and college, is for you to learn about critical thinking skills and perseverance. Using AI will only teach you how to get an answer, which may or may not be correct.

You will not develop the skills needed to problem solve a challenge. Additionally, developing grit is essential to become successful in college and life. There is no easy way out and AI is an illusion to your success in life.


To learn something, it requires hours of work! If not years!

title: Data 300
text:
Trusting AI
When using AI, you must acknowledge its limitations:

Responses provided may be incorrect
Responses may not be fair
Companies may manipulate responses and/or terms of service for their benefit
Companies may not have your best interst in mind


You should always proceed with caution utilizing these tools!

title: Data 300
text:
Stolen Work

Additionally, all these individuals are not receiving any royalties for the work to be used in creating generative AI models.


Inside Higher Ed and The New Yorker highlight individual’s concern of their work being used to train AI models.

title: Data 300
text:
Privacy Concerns
The use of generative AI raises concerns of what data is being harvested from us, possibly without informed consent or knowledge of impacts.

When you use any large language models, you do not know what information is being harvested from you.


Do you want to upload your thoughts and ideas to a company that can monetize, and possibly exploit you.


Does your Professors consent with you uploading their assignments to large language models?


Stanford provided a report highlighting the risks of our personal data use in large language models.

title: Data 300
text:
Environmental Impact
In order to run these large language models, companies need to use a large amounts of energy. This is because large servers are needed to both train and execute a model.

The LA Times reports the potential impact that running AI models in California.


Additionally, Time reports that a ChatGPT query uses ten times more energy than a Google search query, and global AI demands can consume of 1 trillion gallons of water by 2027.


There are also environmental justice questions about where these data centers are constructed.

title: Data 300
text:
Worker Exploitation
The Washington Post and Time (Article 1 and Article 2) reported that AI companies utilize “digital sweatshops” to classify data points for model training.

There is a human cost from the Global South, both financially and mentally, to develop the AI models for users in the United States and Europe.


We must be conscious consumers and demand more from these companies to provide safe working conditions and livable wages.

title: Computational Setup
text:
SQL and Relational Databases
SQL (Structured Query Language) is a language used to work with relational databases.
With SQL, we can:

Retrieve data from tables
Filter and sort records
Summarize data
Combine related tables
Create and modify database objects
Manage data stored in a relational database







Tip


For this course, we will use SQLite as our primary relational database management system (DBMS).

title: Computational Setup
text:
What is SQLite?
SQLite is a lightweight relational database management system.
Unlike many database systems, SQLite does not require a separate database server. A complete database can be stored in a single file, such as:
chinook.db
This makes SQLite useful for:

Learning SQL
Small and medium-sized applications
Local data storage
Prototyping
Reproducible data projects

SQLite

title: Computational Setup
text:
Install SQLite
First, check whether SQLite is already available on your computer.
Open a terminal and run:
sqlite3 --version
If a version number appears, SQLite is installed and available from your terminal.






Note


The exact version number may differ across computers. What matters for this course is that the sqlite3 command runs successfully.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Install SQLite on Windows
Download the command-line tools from the official SQLite download page:
SQLite Download Page
Look for the command-line tools package for your version of Windows.
After downloading:

Extract the files to a folder, such as C:\sqlite.
Add that folder to your Windows PATH.
Open a new terminal.
Run:

sqlite3 --version

title: Computational Setup
text:
Install SQLite on macOS
Many macOS systems already include SQLite.
Check first:
sqlite3 --version
If you use Homebrew and want to install or update SQLite, you can run:
brew install sqlite
Then verify:
sqlite3 --version

title: Computational Setup
text:
Install SQLite on Linux
On Ubuntu or Debian-based systems:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install sqlite3
On Fedora:
sudo dnf install sqlite
Then verify:
sqlite3 --version

title: Computational Setup
text:
Install Positron
Positron is a data science IDE built on Code OSS. We can use it as an editor for SQL files and extend it with database tools.
Download Positron
For this course, we will use Positron or VS Code to:

Organize database project files
Write .sql scripts
Connect to SQLite databases
Run SQL queries
View query results

title: Computational Setup
text:
Install VS Code
Visual Studio Code is a general-purpose code editor that supports database workflows through extensions.
Download VS Code
Recommended extensions for this course:

SQLTools
SQLTools SQLite
Quarto

title: Computational Setup
text:
Install SQLTools
In VS Code or Positron, open the Extensions panel.
Search for and install:

SQLTools (mtxr.sqltools)
SQLTools SQLite (mtxr.sqltools-driver-sqlite)

SQLTools provides the database connection interface. The SQLite driver allows SQLTools to connect specifically to SQLite database files.
SQLTools Documentation






Note


Positron supports VS Code-compatible extensions. Extension availability can depend on the extension catalog configured in Positron.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Workspaces
A workspace is a project folder containing the files needed for a data-management project.
A good workflow is:

Create one folder for the course.
Create a data folder for database files.
Create a sql folder for saved SQL scripts.
Open the course folder in Positron or VS Code.
Connect SQLTools to the SQLite database file.
Save your SQL work in .sql files.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Course Project Files
A simple course folder might look like:
data-management-course/
├── data/
│   └── chinook.db
├── sql/
│   ├── practice.sql
│   └── queries.sql
├── notes/
└── assignments/






Tip


Keeping your database and SQL scripts in the same project folder makes your work easier to organize, reproduce, and submit.

title: Computational Setup
text:
The Chinook Example Database
For examples in this course, we will use the Chinook sample database.
Chinook represents a digital media store and contains related tables for:

Customers
Employees
Invoices
Invoice items
Tracks
Albums
Artists
Genres
Playlists

Chinook Database

title: Computational Setup
text:
Download Chinook for SQLite
Download the SQLite version of the Chinook database from the project releases:
Chinook Releases
The SQLite database file is named similar to:
Chinook_Sqlite.sqlite
For this course, you may rename it:
chinook.db
Place it in your project’s data folder.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Open Chinook from the Terminal
From your course project folder, run:
sqlite3 data/chinook.db
If the database opens successfully, you should see a SQLite prompt similar to:
sqlite>

title: Computational Setup
text:
Useful SQLite Commands
SQLite includes special dot commands for working with the database shell.
Try:
.tables
This displays the tables in the database.
To inspect the structure of the Customer table:
.schema Customer
To exit SQLite:
.quit






Warning


SQLite dot commands such as .tables and .schema are commands for the SQLite shell. They are not SQL statements and should not be included inside SQLTools query scripts.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Create a SQLite Connection
In VS Code or Positron:

Open the Command Palette.
Search for SQLTools: Add New Connection.
Select SQLite as the database driver.
Choose the Chinook database file in your data folder.
Give the connection a name, such as Chinook.
Test and save the connection.

You can now use SQLTools to browse tables and run SQL statements.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Create a SQL File
Inside the sql folder, create a file named:
practice.sql
Use this file to save your SQL statements.
A SQL statement usually ends with a semicolon:
SELECT *
FROM Customer;

title: Computational Setup
text:
View Data from a Table
The SELECT statement retrieves data from a database table.
SELECT *
FROM Customer;
* means to return all columns.
Questions to consider:

What does each row represent?
What does each column represent?
Which column appears to uniquely identify a customer?

title: Computational Setup
text:
Select Specific Columns
Usually, we only select the columns needed for an analysis.
SELECT CustomerId,
       FirstName,
       LastName,
       Country
FROM Customer;
This makes the query output easier to read and reduces unnecessary data retrieval.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Limit Query Results
Use LIMIT when you only want to inspect a small number of rows.
SELECT CustomerId,
       FirstName,
       LastName,
       Country
FROM Customer
LIMIT 10;
This is useful when exploring a table for the first time.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Filter Rows with WHERE
Use WHERE to keep rows that meet a condition.
SELECT CustomerId,
       FirstName,
       LastName,
       Country
FROM Customer
WHERE Country = 'USA';
This returns only customers whose country is the United States.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Comparison Operators
SQL uses comparison operators to define conditions.



Operator
Description




>
Greater than


<
Less than


>=
Greater than or equal


<=
Less than or equal


=
Equal


<> or !=
Not equal



Example:
SELECT InvoiceId,
       CustomerId,
       InvoiceDate,
       Total
FROM Invoice
WHERE Total > 10;

title: Computational Setup
text:
Sort Results
Use ORDER BY to sort query results.
SELECT InvoiceId,
       CustomerId,
       InvoiceDate,
       Total
FROM Invoice
ORDER BY Total DESC;
DESC sorts from largest to smallest.
ASC sorts from smallest to largest and is the default.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Tables, Rows, and Columns
A relational database stores data in tables.
For the Chinook database:

A table represents an entity or relationship, such as Customer or Invoice.
A row represents one record.
A column represents an attribute of that record.

For example, in the Customer table:
CustomerId | FirstName | LastName | Country | Email
Each row represents one customer.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Primary Keys
A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table.
In Chinook, CustomerId is the primary key of the Customer table.
SELECT CustomerId,
       FirstName,
       LastName
FROM Customer
LIMIT 10;
A well-designed primary key should uniquely identify each record.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Foreign Keys
A foreign key connects a row in one table to a related row in another table.
For example, the Invoice table contains CustomerId.
SELECT InvoiceId,
       CustomerId,
       InvoiceDate,
       Total
FROM Invoice
LIMIT 10;
CustomerId connects each invoice to the customer who made the purchase.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Inspect a Table Structure
SQLite’s PRAGMA table_info() command can display information about a table’s columns.
PRAGMA table_info(Customer);
Try the same command for another table:
PRAGMA table_info(Invoice);
Look for:

Column names
Data types
Primary-key indicators
Whether columns allow missing values

title: Computational Setup
text:
View Database Tables with SQL
SQLite stores database metadata in a system table named sqlite_master.
SELECT name,
       type
FROM sqlite_master
WHERE type = 'table'
ORDER BY name;
This is a SQL-based way to inspect which tables exist in the database.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Count Rows
Use COUNT() to count records.
How many customers are in the database?
SELECT COUNT(*) AS number_of_customers
FROM Customer;
The alias number_of_customers gives the result column a meaningful name.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Aggregate Functions
Common SQL aggregate functions include:



Function
Purpose




COUNT()
Count rows or values


SUM()
Add values


AVG()
Calculate a mean


MIN()
Find the minimum


MAX()
Find the maximum



Example:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS number_of_invoices,
       AVG(Total) AS average_invoice,
       MIN(Total) AS smallest_invoice,
       MAX(Total) AS largest_invoice
FROM Invoice;

title: Computational Setup
text:
GROUP BY
Use GROUP BY to calculate summaries for categories.
How many customers are from each country?
SELECT Country,
       COUNT(*) AS number_of_customers
FROM Customer
GROUP BY Country
ORDER BY number_of_customers DESC;
This is a common data-management task: turning row-level records into summarized information.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Why Multiple Tables?
Relational databases usually separate information into multiple related tables rather than storing everything in one large table.
In Chinook:
Artist -> Album -> Track
This design reduces repeated information and allows related records to be managed separately.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Join Two Tables
A JOIN combines related rows from different tables.
SELECT Album.Title AS Album,
       Artist.Name AS Artist
FROM Album
JOIN Artist
  ON Album.ArtistId = Artist.ArtistId
ORDER BY Artist.Name, Album.Title;
The ON clause explains how the tables are related.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Join Tracks to Genres
SELECT Track.Name AS Track,
       Genre.Name AS Genre,
       Track.UnitPrice
FROM Track
JOIN Genre
  ON Track.GenreId = Genre.GenreId
LIMIT 20;
This allows us to retrieve descriptive information stored in separate tables.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Summarize Across Related Tables
Which genres contain the most tracks?
SELECT Genre.Name AS Genre,
       COUNT(Track.TrackId) AS number_of_tracks
FROM Genre
JOIN Track
  ON Genre.GenreId = Track.GenreId
GROUP BY Genre.GenreId, Genre.Name
ORDER BY number_of_tracks DESC;
This query combines:

JOIN
COUNT()
GROUP BY
ORDER BY

title: Computational Setup
text:
Chinook Practice Questions
Use SQLTools and the Chinook database to answer the following questions.

How many tracks are in the Track table?
Which 10 tracks have the highest UnitPrice?
How many customers are from each country?
What are the names of all artists in alphabetical order?
Which albums belong to the artist named AC/DC?
Which genres contain the largest number of tracks?
Which customers have invoices with totals greater than $15?







Tip


Save your answers in a .sql file instead of typing one-time queries that are immediately lost. Saved SQL scripts create a reproducible record of your work.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Data Management Workflow
For database work in this course:

Open the course folder in Positron or VS Code.
Connect SQLTools to data/chinook.db.
Open or create a .sql file.
Write a SQL query.
Run the query and inspect the results.
Revise the query if necessary.
Save the SQL file.

This workflow separates the database from the commands used to analyze it.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Important File Types
You will commonly work with:



File Type
Purpose




.db / .sqlite
SQLite database file


.sql
Saved SQL statements or database scripts


.qmd
Quarto document for notes, lectures, or reports


.csv
Text-based tabular data that may be imported or exported









Warning


Do not edit a .db or .sqlite file as if it were a text file. Use SQLite, SQLTools, or another database client to interact with it.

title: Computational Setup
text:
Database and SQL Resources

SQLite Documentation
SQLite Command-Line Shell
SQLTools Documentation
SQLTools SQLite Driver
Chinook Database
Positron Extensions







Note


The examples in this lecture use SQLite syntax and the Chinook sample database. Later database systems may use slightly different SQL syntax or connection procedures.
